title: Degania, the First Kibbutz
text:
In 1909 a small group of young Jewish immigrants from the Russian Empire was hired to work a farm at Umm Juni, on the southern shore of the Sea of Galilee, then part of the Ottoman Empire. They had come with ideals of returning to the land and living by their own labor. After a year of working under managers, they asked to run the farm themselves, collectively.

In 1910 the group, ten men and two women, founded Degania. They decided that everything would be shared. No one owned private property; work was organized together; income went into a common fund; and decisions were made at a general meeting where every member had a voice. They called it a kvutza, a group.

Life was hard. The land was hot, malaria was common, food was scarce, and the farm faced attacks. The members argued constantly about how to run things. The women had to fight for their place: at first they were expected to cook and wash, and they insisted on working in the fields and the dairy too. Joseph Baratz, one of the founders, later described these early years in his memoir, A Village by the Jordan.

Degania survived. It became the model for hundreds of kibbutzim, collective communities that played a large role in building the state of Israel. One of its first children, Moshe Dayan, was born there in 1915.
lesson: A small group sharing everything needs constant talking, fairness and the willingness to change roles. Equality has to be practiced, not just declared.
people: Joseph Baratz, Miriam Baratz, founders of Degania
location: Degania Alef, near the Sea of Galilee, Israel
source: Joseph Baratz, A Village by the Jordan (1954); kibbutz histories
